title: Street tree inventory
brief:
Write a project proposal for a neighborhood association commissioning an offline street-tree inventory tool for its annual walking survey. Four volunteers use two laptops with no reliable connection during survey shifts. Records need a block name, nearest house number, species or unknown status, observation date, and a short note. The association has 340 existing records in two CSV files with differing headers and possible duplicate entries. It needs spreadsheet export and a printable summary by block. The budget is $1,500, and the survey starts in five weeks. Propose a modest implementation, a migration and reconciliation workflow, testable acceptance criteria, and a training plan for volunteers with basic spreadsheet skills.

Aim for 1,200 to 1,800 words. Return the complete original work directly in your answer. Do not sign or identify yourself. Do not use tools.

18ffb0833f37b5fd.text:
# Project proposal for the annual street-tree inventory

The association can run its walking survey with a small offline desktop application on each of its two laptops. Four volunteers will work in pairs, with one person observing the tree and the other entering the record. Each pair will receive a different set of blocks. A designated survey coordinator will combine the two laptops’ work after each shift and produce the spreadsheet and printed summary from one master inventory.

The proposed fixed price is **$1,500**, including migration of the 340 existing records, installation on both laptops, a field rehearsal, and volunteer training. The application will be ready for that rehearsal in week four, leaving the fifth week for corrections and handoff before the survey starts. The estimate assumes the association supplies both laptops, a USB drive, access to a printer, and a coordinator who can settle questions about local streets and historical records.

## The tool volunteers will use

At the start of a shift, each pair opens the application and selects its first assigned block. The screen lists the trees already recorded there, ordered by nearest house number. A volunteer can select an existing tree and record this year’s observation or choose **Add tree** if the pair finds an additional tree. Keeping existing trees visible matters on streets where several trees share the same species and nearest house number. Volunteers can use a short location note such as “second tree north of driveway” to distinguish them on the next walk.

Each observation requires a block name, nearest house number, species or an explicit **Unknown** selection, and observation date. A note of up to 250 characters is optional. Block names come from a coordinator-maintained list so that spelling variations do not split a block across report lines. The house-number field accepts suffixes such as “24A.” The date defaults to the laptop’s local date and remains editable for observations entered after a walk. Saving returns the volunteer to the same block and shows the saved entry. If a required value is missing, the form keeps the volunteer’s work and identifies the field to complete.

The contractor will package a desktop form backed by a local SQLite database and verify it on the association’s actual laptops. Every tree and observation receives an internal identifier. Updating a known tree adds a dated observation and preserves its earlier history. Correcting a mistaken entry on the same shift updates that observation. Installation, entry, search, export, and printing will all work with wireless access disabled. The scope fits the budget by using the association’s existing street names and block assignments and a standard operating-system print dialog.

## Combining a shift and reporting results

Both laptops start each shift with a copy of the coordinator’s current master inventory. The coordinator records block assignments on a paper shift sheet. Before the pairs leave, each checks its laptop’s date and opens its first block. If a pair runs out of assigned blocks, it checks with the coordinator before moving into another pair’s area.

After the walk, each pair uses **Export shift** to write its changes to the USB drive. The application displays the shift label and observation count, which the pair writes on the shift sheet. The coordinator backs up the master, imports both packages, and compares the import totals with the sheet. Stable identifiers allow a package to be imported twice without doubling the count. If the laptops submit competing changes to the same observation, the import retains both versions for review. The coordinator checks the notes with the volunteers and records the resolution. Both laptops keep their shift data until the coordinator has verified the merge and backup.

The master produces a spreadsheet-compatible CSV with one row per tree, its identifier, and the fields from its latest observation. A separate printable summary uses a selected survey date range and shows each block’s number of distinct trees observed, the number recorded as unknown, and a grand total. A tree visited twice counts once, with species status taken from its latest observation in the range. Blocks with zero observations appear on the report so the coordinator can check them against the shift sheet before declaring the walk complete.

## Migrating and reconciling the 340 records

1. **Preserve and count the source rows.** The contractor will keep untouched copies of both CSV files, count their data rows excluding headers, and check that the combined count is 340. Each row gets a source reference consisting of its filename and original row number. Any count discrepancy goes to the coordinator before the migration proceeds.

2. **Map the headers and inspect exceptions.** The contractor and coordinator will review a short mapping sheet that pairs each source column with an inventory field. They will check examples from both files, including blank species, house numbers with suffixes, and dates whose month and day could be reversed. The import will trim stray spaces and apply agreed block-name spellings while retaining the original values. An ambiguous date or missing address stays on the exception list until the coordinator can resolve it. An undocumented date will never become the migration date.

3. **Review possible duplicates by location.** The contractor will group likely matches using normalized block and house number, with species, observation dates, and notes visible side by side. The coordinator can identify duplicate copies of one observation, separate observations of the same tree, or distinct trees sharing an address. Only confirmed duplicates will be consolidated. If the evidence is inconclusive, the rows stay separately traceable and the coordinator can put the address on the field-check list.

4. **Reconcile and sign off.** The contractor will deliver a worksheet tracing each source row to an imported observation, a confirmed duplicate of another source row, or an unresolved exception. Those three counts must sum to 340. Multiple historical observations may point to one tree. The coordinator will check samples from both files and approve the worksheet, including any outstanding field checks, before the first master inventory is distributed.

## Delivery schedule and budget

| Week | Work and deliverable | Price |
|---|---|---:|
| 1 | Check both laptops and printer, inspect the CSV files, agree on block names and header mapping | $200 |
| 2 | Build and install the offline entry form, block list, local storage, and shift export | $450 |
| 3 | Run the migration, prepare the reconciliation worksheet, and review exceptions with the coordinator | $300 |
| 4 | Complete master import, spreadsheet export, and print layout. Conduct a two-laptop field rehearsal | $350 |
| 5 | Correct rehearsal defects, verify acceptance, train volunteers, and hand over the approved inventory | $200 |
| | **Total** | **$1,500** |

The coordinator’s main time commitment before training is the week-three records review. The contractor will send the candidate matches together so the coordinator can resolve straightforward cases in one sitting and reserve uncertain locations for the walk. The project carries no recurring software fee.

## Acceptance criteria

The coordinator and contractor will use a practice copy for the following checks and record the outcome of each before handoff.

- **Offline operation.** With Wi-Fi disabled on both laptops, each pair opens an assigned block, updates an existing tree, adds a new tree, closes the application, and reopens it. All saved values and the existing tree’s earlier observation are present.
- **Entry validation.** A volunteer saves a tree at “24A” with species marked Unknown and a blank note. Attempts with a missing block, missing house number, unselected species status, or invalid date prompt a correction and preserve the other values entered.
- **Migration accounting.** The worksheet accounts for all 340 source rows. The coordinator can trace a sample row from each file to its destination and trace every consolidation to a recorded decision. Each unresolved row retains its original values and source reference.
- **Shift reconciliation and recovery.** Each laptop exports three new observations from different assigned blocks. Importing both packages adds six observations. Reimporting either adds zero. A separate trial with conflicting edits presents both versions for review. Restoring the pre-import backup to a practice database reproduces the starting counts.
- **Usable outputs.** The coordinator opens the CSV in the association’s spreadsheet program and verifies that a note containing a comma stays in one cell. For a practice survey covering three distinct trees on one block and two on another, including a repeat visit, the printed summary shows block totals of three and two and a grand total of five. The unknown count matches the practice entries, and the report prints without clipped columns.

## Training and handoff

All four volunteers will attend a one-hour session using the survey laptops and practice records. After a ten-minute demonstration, the pairs will spend 25 minutes entering observations and switching roles. Each volunteer will find a known tree, add a second tree near the same house, mark an unfamiliar species Unknown, and correct an entry. The pairs will then spend 15 minutes exporting their shifts and checking the counts as the coordinator combines them. The final ten minutes are for questions and a repeat of any step a volunteer found difficult.

Each laptop will carry a one-page field guide covering shift startup, entry, corrections, and end-of-shift export. The coordinator will also receive the installers, approved master database, original CSV files, reconciliation worksheet, and instructions for backup, restore, and printing. At handoff, the coordinator will independently load the approved inventory on both laptops and print the first block checklist, leaving the equipment ready for the opening shift.

59d30c5c75632dd9.text:
# Project proposal for an offline street-tree inventory

The neighborhood association will commission a small desktop tool for its annual walking survey. Four volunteers will work in two pairs, with one laptop per pair. Each pair can enter, review, and save observations throughout a shift without an internet connection. At the end of the shift, a designated survey coordinator will combine both teams’ work on one laptop and produce a spreadsheet export and a printable summary by block.

The project will cost no more than **$1,500**. The tool, the reconciled historical inventory, and the volunteer training will be ready by the end of week four, leaving week five for a rehearsal and any final fixes before the survey begins.

## What the association will receive

The tool will use a local database and run on the association’s two existing laptops. In the first week, the contractor will confirm the laptops’ operating systems, installation permissions, and ability to exchange files using a USB drive. The association will designate one laptop as the master and one volunteer as the survey coordinator, with a backup coordinator trained to cover the role.

The entry screen will present five fields in walking order.

| Field | Entry and validation |
|---|---|
| Block name | Select from a list approved by the association. The form can keep the previous block selected for the next entry. |
| Nearest house number | Enter the number as text so values such as `12A` are preserved. More than one observation can use the same number. |
| Species or unknown | Enter a species name or explicitly select **Unknown**. |
| Observation date | Defaults to the laptop’s current date and can be corrected before saving. |
| Short note | Optional plain text, limited to 250 characters for new observations. |

Each team can review and correct its current shift’s entries before handing them in. After handoff, corrections go through the coordinator on the master laptop. Each observation receives an internal ID so the tool can recognize a repeated file import even when two trees share a house number.

At the end of each shift, both teams will close their batches. The coordinator will export the second laptop’s batch to a USB drive and import it on the master. The tool will show how many records it added and how many were already present. A failed import will leave the master inventory as it was before the attempt. Once the totals agree with both teams’ handoff counts, the coordinator will make a dated backup on the USB drive. The second laptop will retain its local copy through the end of the survey.

The coordinator can export the master inventory as a CSV that opens in the association’s spreadsheet program. For the printable report, the coordinator selects a date range and prints a summary grouped by block, with observation counts, species counts, and a separate count for unknown species. The report will label its totals as observations. A tree recorded in different years can contribute more than one observation to a report spanning those years.

## Migration and reconciliation

The contractor will preserve both original CSV files and give every source row a reference made from its filename and row number. During week one, the contractor and coordinator will agree on a header map for the five inventory fields. They will also agree on the standard names for blocks and review ambiguous date formats, blank species fields, and any source values that have more than one plausible interpretation.

The contractor will load all 340 rows into a staging worksheet. Straightforward cleanup, such as trimming extra spaces and mapping approved block aliases, will happen there. The worksheet will retain the original values alongside any changes that affect interpretation. Blank species fields will become **Unknown** once the coordinator confirms that this reflects how the old files were kept. Unclear dates, missing house numbers, and unresolved block names will go to a review list. Source notes will be preserved in the migration worksheet if any exceed the new entry limit.

The contractor will flag two kinds of possible duplicate. The first is a pair of rows whose fields agree after cleanup. The second is a pair with the same block, house number, and date but differences in species or notes. The coordinator will review the source rows side by side and decide whether they describe the same observation, separate observations, or a case that needs more information. Matching addresses alone will never trigger a merge. When the coordinator confirms a duplicate, the retained record will keep both source references in the migration log and preserve any distinct information the coordinator approves.

Before loading the master inventory, the contractor will deliver a reconciliation worksheet that accounts for all 340 source rows. Each row will be marked as imported, linked to a retained record as a confirmed duplicate, or held for a documented reason. Held rows will stay in the worksheet for later resolution. The coordinator will approve the worksheet and compare a sample from each source file against the master export. The same review process will apply to possible overlaps between walking teams, with batch and record counts checked before any duplicate is resolved.

## Schedule and fixed budget

| Week | Work and milestone | Cost |
|---|---|---:|
| 1 | Check both laptops, review CSV headers and sample rows, agree on the block list and field rules. | $200 |
| 2 | Build the offline entry screen, shift review, batch transfer, CSV export, and block report. | $625 |
| 3 | Stage all 340 rows, prepare the duplicate review, and load the approved inventory after coordinator review. | $300 |
| 4 | Run acceptance checks on both laptops, train all four volunteers, and hand over the tool and documentation. | $250 |
| 5 | Run a short practice walk and address any issues that would prevent survey use. | $125 |
| | **Total** | **$1,500** |

The estimate assumes the association supplies the two laptops, a USB drive, and access to its usual spreadsheet and printing setup. It also assumes the coordinator is available in week one to confirm field interpretations and in week three to decide flagged migration cases. If a historical row still needs research when the survey starts, it can remain in the reconciliation worksheet while the master inventory and survey proceed. The price includes the installed tool, source code and installation instructions, the migration worksheet and log, and a one-page volunteer guide. The tool requires no paid subscription.

## Acceptance criteria

The contractor and coordinator will run the following checks using the actual laptops and the association’s spreadsheet and printing setup. They will use practice data for the survey exercises and keep it separate from the live inventory.

| Check | Passing result |
|---|---|
| Offline operation | With Wi-Fi off on both laptops, each team can open the tool, enter and edit observations, close it, reopen it, and find all saved entries. |
| Field handling | The form requires a block, house number, species or **Unknown**, and a valid date. It accepts a house number such as `12A`, an empty note, and two distinct observations at the same address. It flags a new note over 250 characters without clearing the form. |
| Shift consolidation | With 10 practice observations entered on each laptop, the coordinator closes both batches and produces a master inventory with all 20. Importing the same transfer file again leaves the total at 20. An invalid transfer file leaves the count and existing records unchanged. |
| Historical migration | The reconciliation worksheet accounts for exactly 340 source rows. Every confirmed duplicate links to a retained record, every held row has a reason, and spot checks from both CSVs match the approved worksheet. The master’s historical count equals the number of rows marked as imported. |
| Spreadsheet export | The CSV opens in the association’s spreadsheet program with the five survey fields in separate columns. The exported row count matches the inventory, and a test note containing a comma and quotation marks stays in one cell. |
| Printable report | For a practice survey with known counts across two blocks, the selected date range produces the expected block, species, unknown, and overall totals. A printed page or print preview has legible headings and no clipped columns. |
| Backup and recovery | The coordinator restores a dated backup into a separate practice copy and verifies that its record count and sampled observations match the master at the time of backup. |

## Volunteer training and handover

Week four includes a one-hour hands-on session for all four volunteers. The first 10 minutes cover how to choose a block, identify the nearest house number, and use **Unknown** when a species cannot be identified confidently. For the next 25 minutes, volunteers work in pairs with Wi-Fi off. Each person takes a turn entering records, including two trees at the same address, then finds and corrects one saved entry. This gives each pair practice switching between observing and typing during a walk.

The final 25 minutes cover shift handoff. The volunteers compare their batch counts, then the coordinator imports the second laptop’s file, checks the combined total, saves a backup, and produces the spreadsheet and report. The backup coordinator repeats the transfer and verifies that importing the same file again adds zero records. The one-page guide will show the order of these steps and where the association keeps transfer files and backups.

During the week-five practice walk, each pair will complete a short route and hand in a batch using the guide. The project is ready for survey use when both pairs can complete that exercise and either coordinator can consolidate the records, back up the master, and produce the block report without contractor assistance.
